title: Business Communication
subtitle: Write and speak so that clients, suppliers and partners understand you the first time, reply quickly and trust you.
description: A practical course in everyday business communication for women running or growing a business in Nigeria and across Africa. You will learn clear writing, the right tone, emails, WhatsApp Business messages, formal letters, invoices and receipts, meetings and minutes, phone manners, negotiation and cross-cultural communication, with many before-and-after examples. You finish with a real business message, measured results and a 90-day plan.
outcomes: Write purpose-first emails, WhatsApp messages and letters in a tone that suits the reader
Produce clear quotations, invoices, receipts and payment reminders that get paid
Handle business calls, voice notes and complaints calmly and professionally
Run a focused meeting and write action minutes with owners and deadlines
Prepare for and conduct a basic negotiation and confirm the agreement in writing
Adapt your communication for different cultures, languages and time zones
audience: Women who run or work in small businesses, cooperatives and organisations and want to communicate more professionally with customers, suppliers and partners.
tools: A smartphone with WhatsApp Business installed
An email account (a free Gmail account is fine)
A notebook and pen, or a notes or spreadsheet app
A free document app such as Google Docs for letters, invoices and minutes

modules.title: Foundations: Clear Writing, the Right Tone and the Phone
modules.overview: Every business message, from a WhatsApp reply to a formal letter, rests on the same three habits: say what you want early, use plain words, and match your tone to the reader. This module builds those habits and applies them to the most common business channel of all, the phone call.

lessons.title: Clear business writing: purpose first, plain words
objectives: Put the main point of a message in the first one or two sentences
Replace long, vague phrases with short, plain words
Write sentences in the active voice so it is clear who does what
Rewrite an unclear message using the before-and-after method

blocks.text: Business readers are busy. A supplier, a customer or a programme officer often reads your message on a small phone screen, between other tasks. If they cannot see within a few seconds **what you want and by when**, your message waits, or it is misunderstood. Clear writing is not about big English. It is about making the reader's job easy.

blocks.name: compose-email
blocks.alt: A woman composing a message on a screen
blocks.caption: Before you type, decide the one thing you want the reader to know or do.

blocks.text: Rule 1: Main point first

Many of us were taught to build up slowly: greetings, background, history, and only at the end the request. In business, turn this around. Put the **purpose and the request in the first one or two sentences**, then give only the background the reader needs. Some writers call this BLUF, short for "bottom line up front". The polite greeting still comes first, but it stays short.
Rule 2: Plain words and short sentences

Plain language means words your reader understands the first time. Government plain-language guides, such as the United States plainlanguage.gov guidelines, recommend short sentences, everyday words, and speaking directly to the reader as "you". This matters even more when your reader speaks English as a second or third language, which is common across Nigeria and Africa. Aim for sentences of about 15 to 20 words, and one idea per sentence.

head: Instead of this
Write this
rows: We wish to bring to your kind attention that
kindly revert at your earliest convenience
we are in receipt of your letter

blocks.text: Notice the last two rows. "Do the needful" and "revert" are common in Nigerian offices, but they hide the actual action. A reader from another country may not understand "revert" as "reply" at all. Always name the exact action and, where possible, a date.
Rule 3: Active voice

In the **active voice**, the person doing the action comes first: "Chika will deliver the chairs on Monday." In the **passive voice**, the doer is hidden or comes last: "The chairs will be delivered." By whom? Passive sentences are not always wrong, but in business they often hide responsibility. Use the active voice when you want someone to act.

blocks.title: Plan a clear message in four moves
items: Who is reading?
What must they do?
Main point first
Check and cut
blocks.caption: Decide reader and action before writing, lead with the point, then cut every word that does not help.

blocks.title: Worked example: a message to a hall manager, before and after
blocks.context: For example, Funke runs a small events business in Ibadan. She needs to confirm a hall booking for a client's birthday party and wants the hall manager to send the invoice.
steps: Before (68 words): "Good afternoon sir, I hope this message finds you well. I am writing in respect of the discussion we had last week concerning the possibility of using your hall for an event which a client of mine is planning towards the end of the month, and I wanted to find out whether it would be possible for you to kindly do the needful regarding the invoice at your earliest convenience."
Problem 1: the request (send the invoice) is hidden at the very end.
Problem 2: no date, no hall name, no number of guests, so the manager must call back to ask.
Problem 3: "do the needful" and "at your earliest convenience" give no clear action or deadline.

After (45 words): "Good afternoon Mr Bello. Please send me the invoice for the Main Hall for Saturday 29 March, 2pm to 8pm, for about 120 guests. My client will pay the deposit once I receive it. Could you send it by Wednesday? Thank you, Funke Adeyemi, 0803 000 0000."
blocks.result: The second version is shorter, puts the request first, and gives every detail the manager needs to act without calling back.

blocks.title: The phone-screen test
blocks.text: Before you send, imagine your reader sees only the first two lines in their notification. Would they know what you want? If not, move your request up.
A quick self-check before you send

items: Can I say my purpose in one sentence? Is that sentence near the top?
Have I named exact dates, amounts, quantities and places?
Is every sentence under about 20 words?
Have I replaced vague phrases such as "do the needful" with the actual action?
Have I read it once from the reader's side, asking: what would I still need to ask?

blocks.text: Short paragraphs and lists

On a phone screen, a paragraph of ten lines looks like a wall of text, and readers skip it. Keep paragraphs to about three or four lines. When you give several items, such as sizes, dates or documents, put them in a short list. A list lets the reader tick off each point, and it makes it obvious if something is missing. For example, "Please bring: 1. CAC certificate, 2. a valid ID, 3. two passport photos" is easier to act on than the same items buried in a long sentence.

takeaways: Put the purpose and the request in the first one or two sentences.
Plain, short words are more professional than long, formal ones.
Name the exact action, date, amount and place.
Use the active voice when you need someone to act.
Read your draft from the reader's side before sending.

activity.title: Rewrite one real message
steps: Find a business message you sent in the last month (WhatsApp, SMS or email).
Copy it into your notebook and count the words.
Underline the actual request. Note where it appears.
Rewrite it with the request in the first two sentences and all key details named.
Count the words again and compare the two versions.
activity.evidence: A notebook page or screenshot showing the before and after versions with word counts

lessons.title: Choosing the right tone and level of formality
objectives: Place a reader on a formality ladder from close contact to formal institution
Use titles, greetings and sign-offs that suit the relationship
Turn a demanding message into a firm but polite one
Avoid tone mistakes common in text-based messages

blocks.text: Tone is how your message sounds in the reader's head. The same request can sound respectful, cold, pushy or desperate depending on the words around it. In person, your smile and voice soften your words. In writing, the reader only has the words, so tone must be built in on purpose.

blocks.name: business-chat
blocks.caption: The same request can land well or badly depending on tone.

blocks.text: The formality ladder

Think of formality as a ladder. At the bottom are people you know well and deal with often. At the top are people and organisations you are meeting for the first time, or who have authority over a decision you need. **The higher the step, the more formal you write.** When you are not sure, start one step higher, then follow the other person's lead once they reply.

blocks.title: The formality ladder
items: Government, banks, first contact
New clients and partners
Regular suppliers and customers
Team members you know well
blocks.caption: Read from the top: the higher the step, the more formal your greeting, wording and sign-off.

head: Step
Greeting
Sign-off
Style
rows: Dear Sir or Madam, or Dear Mrs Okafor
Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely, full name and role
Full sentences, no abbreviations, no emojis
Dear Mr Musa, or Good morning Mr Musa
Kind regards, full name, business name, phone
Good morning Mama Tunde, or Hello Emeka
Friendly, short, still clear on details
Brief, but still clear about the task and deadline

blocks.text: Titles and respect in the Nigerian setting

Titles carry real weight in many Nigerian and African business settings. If someone signs as Dr, Chief, Alhaji, Engr. or Barrister, use that title until they invite you to drop it. With an older person or a senior official, "Sir" or "Ma" in a spoken conversation is normal and polite. In a written email, "Dear Dr Okeke" carries the same respect without repeating "sir" in every line. When writing to someone abroad, use Mr or Ms with their surname unless they sign with a first name only.
Firm is not the same as rude

Sometimes you must ask for something difficult: late payment, a missed delivery, a wrong order. You can be firm without being rude. A firm message states the facts, the effect, and the exact next step. A rude message attacks the person, uses capital letters to shout, or makes threats you will not carry out.

blocks.title: Worked example: chasing a late delivery, three tones
blocks.context: For example, Amina ordered 50 branded tote bags from a printer in Kano for a conference. The printer promised delivery on Monday. It is now Wednesday and nothing has arrived.
steps: Too soft: "Good day sir, sorry to disturb you, please whenever you have time, maybe you can check on the bags? No problem if not." The printer reads this as "not urgent".
Too harsh: "WHERE ARE MY BAGS?? You people are never serious. If they don't come today I will report you everywhere." The printer becomes defensive, and the relationship is damaged.

Firm and polite: "Good morning Mr Sani. The 50 tote bags (order 112) were due on Monday and have not arrived. The conference starts on Saturday, so I need them by Thursday 5pm. Can you confirm today whether that is possible? Thank you."
The firm version gives the order number, the original date, the reason for urgency, a clear deadline and a direct question that needs an answer today.
blocks.result: The printer replies with a real delivery time instead of an excuse, and Amina keeps a supplier she may need again.

blocks.title: Text loses your smile
blocks.text: Short replies such as "Ok." or "Noted." can read as cold or annoyed, even when you are just busy. Add a few words: "Noted, thank you. I will send it by 4pm." Avoid all capital letters, many exclamation marks, and emojis in first contact or formal messages.
Match, then lead

A useful habit is to **match the other person's level**, then lead slightly towards clarity. If a new partner writes "Dear Mrs Eze", reply with "Dear Mr Daniel", not "Hi!". If a long-time customer sends a voice note in Pidgin, a friendly reply in simple English or Pidgin is fine, but put the price, quantity and delivery day in clear written text so there is a record. Being friendly and being exact are not opposites.
Saying no and apologising politely

Two of the hardest tone moments are refusing a request and admitting a mistake. In both cases, be brief, warm and specific. Thank the person, give the answer clearly, give a short reason if it helps, and offer an alternative where you can. Avoid long, nervous explanations; they make a simple no sound uncertain.

items: Refusing a discount: "Thank you for asking. Our price for this order is fixed at ₦45,000, but delivery within Ikeja is free."
Declining a job: "Thank you for thinking of us. We are fully booked that weekend, but I can recommend a colleague."
Apologising: "I am sorry, I sent the wrong invoice. The correct one is attached and the total is ₦32,000."

takeaways: The newer or more senior the reader, the more formal you write.
When unsure, start one step more formal and follow their lead.
Use the titles people use for themselves.
Firm messages state facts, effect and next step, without insults or threats.
Very short replies can sound cold; add a few warm, clear words.

activity.title: Map your contacts on the ladder
steps: List ten people or organisations you message for business.
Place each one on a step of the formality ladder.
For three of them, write the greeting and sign-off you will use from now on.
Pick one message you need to send this week that requires firmness, and write it using facts, effect and next step.
activity.evidence: A list of ten contacts with their ladder step, plus one firm-but-polite draft

lessons.title: Phone calls and voice notes that sound professional
objectives: Answer a business call with a clear, professional greeting
Plan an outgoing call with a short three-part script
Leave a voicemail or voice note that the listener can act on
Confirm what was agreed on a call in a short written follow-up

blocks.text: For many small businesses in Nigeria, the phone is still the main business tool. Customers call to ask prices, suppliers call about deliveries, and partners prefer a quick call to a long email. A well-handled call builds trust fast. A rushed or confusing call can lose a sale in under a minute.

blocks.name: talking-on-the-phone
blocks.alt: A woman talking on a mobile phone
blocks.caption: A calm, clear phone manner builds trust before the customer ever meets you.

blocks.text: Answering a business call

When a call comes to your business line, answer within a few rings with three things: a greeting, your business name and your own name. For example: "Good morning, Bisi's Bakes, this is Bisi speaking. How can I help you?" This tells the caller they reached the right place and who they are speaking to. If you are in a noisy market or driving, it is more professional to let the call go and call back within the hour than to shout "I can't hear you!".

items: Greet, give the business name and your name.
Listen to the full request without interrupting.
Repeat the key details back: "So that is two dozen cupcakes for Friday at 10am?"
Agree the next step: price, payment method, delivery time.
Close politely and say what happens next: "I will send the invoice on WhatsApp in ten minutes."

blocks.text: Making a call: the three-part script

Before you call a supplier, client or official, write three short lines: **who you are, why you are calling, and what you need from them**. Keep your notebook and any order numbers in front of you. This avoids the common problem of talking for five minutes and ending the call without the answer you needed.

blocks.title: A well-run business call
items: Prepare three lines
Greet and introduce
State purpose
Agree next step
Send written follow-up
blocks.caption: The call is not finished until the agreement is in writing.

blocks.title: Worked example: calling a fabric supplier
blocks.context: For example, Esther makes school uniforms in Aba and needs to confirm a price before she quotes a school.
steps: Her three lines: "Esther, Uniform Works, ordered from you in January. Calling to confirm the price of navy gabardine for 300 yards. I need the price and delivery date today so I can quote a school."
On the call: "Good afternoon, this is Esther from Uniform Works. I bought navy gabardine from you in January. I am calling to confirm your current price for 300 yards and how soon you can deliver."
The supplier says about ₦2,500 per yard (an illustrative price), delivery in five days.
Esther repeats it back: "So 300 yards at ₦2,500, that is ₦750,000 in total, delivered by next Tuesday?"
Within ten minutes she sends a WhatsApp message: "Thank you for the call. Confirming: 300 yards navy gabardine at ₦2,500 per yard, total ₦750,000, delivery by Tuesday 18 March. Please confirm."
blocks.result: Esther now has a written record she can rely on when she quotes the school, and any misunderstanding about price is caught before money moves.

blocks.text: Voicemails and voice notes

Voice notes on WhatsApp are fast and personal, and many customers prefer them. But a three-minute voice note is hard to search, hard to listen to in a meeting, and impossible to skim. Keep business voice notes **under about one minute**, say the main point first, and follow up any numbers, addresses or account details in text. For a voicemail, say your name, business, reason for calling and phone number slowly, and repeat the number at the end.

head: Do
Avoid
rows: Main point in the first sentence
Several long voice notes in a row
Numbers and addresses also sent in text
Prices or account numbers only in audio
Recording in heavy traffic or a loud market

blocks.title: Phone scams
blocks.text: Never share your BVN, card PIN, OTP codes or online banking password on a call, even if the caller says they are from your bank. Banks do not ask for these. End the call and phone your bank on the number printed on your card or their official website.
Taking a message for someone else
If a call is for a colleague or partner who is not available, never just say "She is not around" and end the call. Take a proper message so that nothing is lost.

items: Say politely that the person is not available and offer to take a message.
Write down the caller's full name and business, and spell names back if unsure.
Write the phone number and read it back digit by digit.
Note the reason for the call and how urgent it is.
Tell the caller when they can expect a call back, and pass the message on in writing straight away.

blocks.text: Finally, if you miss a business call, return it the same day where possible. A quick message such as "Sorry I missed your call, I am in a meeting until 3pm. Can I call you then?" keeps the customer warm.

takeaways: Answer with greeting, business name and your name.
Plan every important call with three lines: who, why, what you need.
Repeat key details back before the call ends.
Keep voice notes short and put numbers in text.
Confirm every phone agreement in a written follow-up.

activity.title: Script and follow up one real call
steps: Choose a business call you need to make this week.
Write your three-line script: who you are, why you are calling, what you need.
Make the call and repeat the key details back before you end it.
Send a written follow-up within one hour confirming what was agreed.
Note how the other person responded to the follow-up.
activity.evidence: Your three-line script and a screenshot of the written follow-up message

quiz.q: Kemi needs a caterer to confirm a quote for Saturday. Where should her request go in the message?
options: At the end, after explaining the whole event
In the first one or two sentences, after a short greeting
In a second message sent the next day
Only in the subject line, with no body text
quiz.explain: Putting the purpose and request first means the reader sees it immediately, even in a phone notification.

quiz.q: Which rewrite of "Kindly do the needful at your earliest convenience" is clearest?
options: Please send the signed contract by Thursday 20 March
We look forward to your kind cooperation
quiz.explain: It names the exact action and the deadline, so the reader knows precisely what to do.

quiz.q: You are writing to a bank's business desk for the first time. Which greeting fits best?
quiz.explain: A formal institution and first contact sit at the top of the formality ladder, so a formal greeting is right.

quiz.q: A supplier is two days late. Which message is firm but polite?
options: Sorry to disturb, whenever you can please check
Order 45 was due Monday and has not arrived. I need it by Thursday 5pm. Can you confirm today?
I will report you if it does not come
quiz.explain: It states the facts, the deadline and a direct question, without insults or threats.

quiz.q: After agreeing a price on the phone with a supplier, what should you do next?
options: Nothing, a phone agreement is enough
Send a short written message confirming the quantity, price and date
Call again the next day to check they remember
Wait for the supplier to send an invoice
quiz.explain: A written follow-up creates a record and catches any misunderstanding before money moves.

quiz.q: Which voice note habit is most professional?
options: Several three-minute notes in a row
Main point first, under about a minute, with numbers also sent in text
Recording while walking through a busy market
quiz.explain: Short, point-first notes with key numbers in text are easy to act on and keep a searchable record.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Emails, WhatsApp and Business Letters
modules.overview: Now you apply the foundations to the three written channels you will use most. You will build professional emails, set up and write WhatsApp Business messages that customers trust, and lay out a formal business letter correctly.

lessons.title: Writing professional emails that get replies
objectives: Write a specific subject line that tells the reader what the email is about
Structure an email body as greeting, purpose, details, request and signature
Use To, CC and BCC correctly
Set up a professional email signature and handle attachments properly

blocks.text: Email is still the main formal channel for banks, grant programmes, larger companies, government agencies and international buyers. When you apply for a contract, send a quotation to a corporate client or reply to a training programme, your email is often the first thing they see of your business. A clear, well-built email makes a small business look organised and reliable.

blocks.name: email
blocks.alt: An open email on a laptop screen
blocks.caption: A clear subject line and a purpose-first opening help your email get read and answered.

blocks.text: The subject line

The subject line decides whether and when your email is opened. Make it **specific**: what it is about and, if needed, what you want. "Hello" or "Enquiry" tells the reader nothing. "Quotation request: 200 branded mugs, needed by 30 April" tells them everything before they open it.

head: Weak subject
Strong subject
rows: Introduction: Ada's Catering, lunch packs for staff events
Request for invoice: Main Hall booking, 29 March
Action needed by Friday: signed supply agreement
CAC certificate and tax ID for vendor registration

blocks.text: The body: five parts

blocks.title: The five parts of a business email
items: Greeting
Purpose sentence
Key details
Clear request
Signature
blocks.caption: Every business email can follow this order, from a two-line note to a full proposal cover email.

items: Greeting: "Dear Mrs Okoro," for formal, "Good morning Tunde," for a known contact.
Purpose sentence: one sentence saying why you are writing.
Key details: only what the reader needs, using short paragraphs or a short list.
Clear request: what you want them to do and by when, ideally as a question.
Closing and signature: "Kind regards," then your full name, role, business name, phone number.

blocks.text: To, CC and BCC

Put the person who must **act** in the To line. Put people who only need to **know** in CC (carbon copy). Use BCC (blind carbon copy) when you email many people who do not know each other, such as customers, so that their addresses stay private. Sending a group email to 50 customers with every address visible in the To line exposes their contact details to everyone on the list. Before you click Reply All, ask whether everyone really needs your reply.

blocks.title: Worked example: a first email to a potential corporate client
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a small catering business in Lagos and has been told that a logistics company buys lunch packs for staff training days.
steps: Subject: "Lunch packs for staff training days: menu and price list attached"
Greeting: "Dear Mrs Adebayo,"
Purpose: "Mr Kola Ojo of your HR team suggested I contact you about lunch packs for your monthly staff training days."

Details: "We supply packed lunches for groups of 20 to 150 in Lagos Mainland. Our standard pack is jollof rice, chicken and a drink, about ₦3,500 per pack at current prices. We have served three corporate clients this year. Our menu and price list are attached as one PDF."
Request: "Could we arrange a free tasting for two members of your team next week? I am available Tuesday or Thursday afternoon."
Signature: "Kind regards, Ngozi Eze, Founder, Ngozi's Kitchen, 0805 000 0000, CAC-registered business."
blocks.result: In about 110 words, Mrs Adebayo knows who referred Ngozi, what she offers, the price range and exactly what Ngozi is asking for.

blocks.text: Attachments and signature

items: Mention every attachment in the body: "I have attached our price list (PDF)."
Name files clearly: NgozisKitchen_PriceList_March.pdf, not IMG_2045.jpg.
Send PDFs for documents you do not want changed; keep files small for readers on mobile data.
Set up a signature once in your email app with full name, role, business name, phone and, if you have one, website.
Use an email address with your name or business name. A free Gmail address such as ngozis.kitchen@gmail.com is fine; a professional domain address is better when you can afford it.

blocks.title: Proofread out loud
blocks.text: Read important emails out loud before sending. Your ear catches missing words and long sentences that your eyes skip. Check names, amounts and dates twice, and make sure the attachment is actually attached.
Replying and following up

Professional email works both ways. When you receive an important email, reply within one working day, even if only to say you received it and when you will give a full answer: "Thank you, I have received the tender documents and will send our quotation by Thursday." When you send an important email and hear nothing, do not assume the answer is no. People are busy and emails get buried.

blocks.title: Worked example: a polite follow-up email
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sent her introduction email on Monday and has had no reply by the following Monday.
steps: She replies in the same email thread so Mrs Adebayo can see the first message.
Subject stays the same, so the thread is easy to find.

Body: "Dear Mrs Adebayo, I am following up on my email below about lunch packs for your staff training days. Would a short call this week be easier than a tasting? I am free Wednesday or Friday morning. Kind regards, Ngozi."
blocks.result: The follow-up is short, polite, gives an easier option and keeps the full history in one place.

takeaways: A specific subject line is the first step to a reply.
Follow the five parts: greeting, purpose, details, request, signature.
To is for action, CC is for information, BCC protects private addresses.
Mention and clearly name every attachment.
Proofread names, amounts and dates before sending.

activity.title: Build a complete business email
steps: Choose a real business contact you need to email this month.
Write a specific subject line.
Draft the body using the five parts.
Set up or update your email signature.
Read the email out loud, fix what you hear, then send it or save it as a draft.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of the finished email, showing subject line, body and signature

lessons.title: WhatsApp Business messages customers trust
objectives: Set up the main WhatsApp Business app tools: profile, catalogue, greeting, away message and quick replies
Write customer replies that answer price, availability and delivery in one message
Use broadcast lists respectfully and with consent
Keep clear written records of orders agreed on WhatsApp

blocks.text: For many small businesses across Africa, WhatsApp is the shop window, the order book and the customer service desk all in one. Customers decide in seconds whether you are serious. A clear profile and fast, complete replies win orders. Late, vague or pushy messages lose them.

blocks.name: messaging-app
blocks.alt: A phone showing a chat conversation
blocks.caption: Your WhatsApp profile and replies are often a customer's first experience of your business.

blocks.text: Set up the WhatsApp Business app properly

WhatsApp Business is a separate, free app from the ordinary WhatsApp. It is designed for small businesses and includes tools the personal app does not have. Set these up once and they work for you every day.

head: Tool
What it does
Example use
rows: Shows your business name, category, address, hours, email and website
Customers see you are a real business with opening hours
Lets you list products or services with photos, descriptions and prices
Customers browse your cakes or hairstyles without asking for pictures
Sends an automatic welcome to new customers
"Welcome to Bisi's Bakes. Our menu is in the catalogue. How can we help?"
"We are closed now. We open 8am to 6pm, Monday to Saturday, and will reply then."
Saved answers you call up by typing / and a shortcut
/price sends your price list, /bank sends payment details
Tags chats such as New order, Paid, Delivered
You can see at a glance who still owes payment

blocks.text: The complete reply

Most customer enquiries ask the same few questions: Is it available? How much? How do I pay? When can I get it? A **complete reply** answers all four in one message, so the customer can decide without a long back and forth. Every extra message you make them send is a chance for them to buy elsewhere.

blocks.title: A complete customer reply
items: Greet by name
Confirm availability
Give price and options
Explain payment and delivery
Ask one clear question
blocks.caption: One message that covers these five points usually turns an enquiry into an order.

blocks.title: Worked example: answering "How much?", before and after
blocks.context: For example, Halima sells hand-made bead necklaces from Abuja. A new customer sends: "Hello, how much is the blue necklace in your status?"
steps: Before: "8k". The customer must now ask about delivery, payment and whether it is still available, and may simply leave.

After: "Good afternoon Joy, thank you for asking. Yes, the blue beaded necklace is available. It is ₦8,000. Matching earrings are ₦3,000 extra. Delivery within Abuja is about ₦2,000 and takes 1 to 2 days. You can pay by bank transfer and I will send the account details. Would you like the necklace alone or with the earrings?"
The customer replies: "With earrings please."
Halima confirms in writing: "Great. Order: blue necklace ₦8,000 + earrings ₦3,000 + delivery ₦2,000 = ₦13,000. Please send your delivery address and phone number."
blocks.result: One complete reply and one written confirmation turn a two-word enquiry into a confirmed ₦13,000 order with no confusion about the total.

blocks.text: Broadcasts, status and respect

A **broadcast list** sends one message to many customers, each receiving it as a private chat. Broadcast messages only reach people who have saved your number in their phone, which is WhatsApp's built-in way of keeping broadcasts to people who know you. Use broadcasts for genuine news: new stock, price changes, holiday hours. Sending several promotions a day, or adding people to groups without asking, quickly leads to people blocking or reporting your number.

blocks.title: Payment and privacy safety on WhatsApp
blocks.text: Never deliver goods on the strength of a screenshot of a transfer alone; check your own banking app or SMS alert from your bank. Never send customers' phone numbers or addresses to other people. Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp settings so no one can take over your business account with a stolen code.
Keep the record

items: Confirm every order in one written message with items, quantities, total, payment method and delivery date.
Use labels such as New order, Awaiting payment, Paid, Delivered.
Star important messages such as payment confirmations so you can find them later.
Reply within your stated hours; if you need time, say so: "Let me check stock and reply by 3pm."

blocks.text: Groups, status and opening hours

WhatsApp Status is a good place to show new products, behind-the-scenes photos and customer feedback (with permission). Keep each post clear: one product, the price, and how to order. For customer groups, only add people who have agreed to join, explain the purpose of the group in its description, and set clear rules, such as "announcements only". Finally, respect your own stated hours. Replying at midnight once may please one customer, but it teaches everyone to expect it. Your away message does the polite work for you.

takeaways: Set up your business profile, catalogue, greeting, away message and quick replies once.
A complete reply answers availability, price, payment and delivery in one message.
Always confirm orders with a written summary and total.
Use broadcasts for real news, not constant promotion.
Check payments in your own banking app before delivering.

activity.title: Upgrade your WhatsApp Business setup
steps: Install or open the WhatsApp Business app and complete your business profile.
Add at least three products or services to your catalogue with prices.
Write and switch on a greeting message and an away message.
Create two quick replies: one for prices and one for payment and delivery.
Rewrite your usual answer to "How much?" as a complete reply.

lessons.title: Formal business letters and getting feedback on your writing
objectives: Lay out a formal business letter in full block format
Choose the correct salutation and complimentary close
Write a letter of enquiry or complaint that is clear and courteous
Use a simple peer-review checklist to improve important messages before sending

blocks.text: Formal letters are still required for many important business moments: applying to a bank or grant programme, writing to a local government office, introducing your business to a school or hospital, making a formal complaint, or confirming an agreement. A correctly laid out letter tells the reader you understand professional standards.

blocks.name: letter
blocks.alt: A formal letter in an envelope
blocks.caption: A correctly laid out letter shows you understand professional standards.

blocks.text: Full block format

The most common modern layout is **full block format**: every line starts at the left margin, with a blank line between parts and no indented paragraphs. It is easy to type on a phone or computer and looks neat. Many writers in Nigeria were taught a semi-block style with the address on the right; both are acceptable, but block format is simpler and widely used.

blocks.title: Parts of a block-format letter, top to bottom
items: Your address and date
Recipient's name and address
Salutation and subject line
Body paragraphs
Close, signature, name
blocks.caption: Every part starts at the left margin, with one blank line between parts.

head: Part
What to write
rows: Business name, street, town, state, phone, email
Written in full: 14 March 2025, not 14/3/25, to avoid confusion between day-first and month-first readers
Dear Mrs Okafor, or Dear Sir or Madam, if you do not know the name
One line in bold or capitals: APPLICATION FOR SUPPLIER REGISTRATION
Opening paragraph with purpose, one or two paragraphs of details, closing paragraph with request
Yours sincerely or Yours faithfully, then signature, full name and role

blocks.text: Sincerely or faithfully?

In British-style English, which Nigerian business writing generally follows, the rule is simple: if you began with the person's **name** ("Dear Mr Bello"), end with **"Yours sincerely"**. If you began with **"Dear Sir or Madam"**, end with **"Yours faithfully"**. American writers often use "Sincerely" for both. Whichever you use, be consistent.

blocks.title: Worked example: a complaint letter, before and after
blocks.context: For example, Grace owns a small printing shop in Enugu. A generator she bought from a dealer stopped working after two weeks, and her calls have not been answered.
steps: Before: "I am very disappointed with your company. The generator you sold me is useless and I want my money back immediately or I will take action." No date of purchase, no receipt number, no model, no clear request.
After, opening paragraph: "I am writing about a 3.5 kVA generator, receipt number 0458, which I bought from your Ogui Road branch on 2 March 2025."

Details paragraph: "The generator stopped starting on 16 March. I called your branch on 17 and 18 March and was told a technician would visit, but no one has come. A copy of the receipt and the warranty card is enclosed."
Request paragraph: "Please arrange a repair or replacement under the warranty by Friday 28 March. You can reach me on 0807 000 0000."
Close: "Yours faithfully," signature, "Grace Nwosu, Owner, Grace Prints", because she opened with "Dear Sir or Madam".
blocks.result: The second letter gives the dealer every fact needed to act, names a fair remedy and deadline, and is calm enough that it can later be shown to a consumer-protection office if needed.

blocks.text: Getting feedback before you send

For high-stakes writing, such as a grant application, a large quotation or a complaint, ask a trusted person to read it first. Do not just ask "Is it fine?". Give them specific questions, so their feedback is useful.

items: After reading only the first paragraph, what do you think I want?
Is any word, phrase or abbreviation unclear?
Is anything missing that you would need to reply?
Does the tone feel respectful, too soft, or too harsh?
Are names, dates and amounts consistent everywhere?

blocks.title: Watch the replies you get
blocks.text: Your readers give you feedback every day. If people often reply with questions such as "Which date?" or "How much in total?", your first messages are missing details. Note these questions and add the answers to your next messages before anyone has to ask.
Common business letters and how to open them

head: Letter type
Typical purpose
First sentence example
rows: Ask for information, prices or terms
I am writing to ask about your prices for supplying 500 exercise books each term.
Apply for a contract, grant, loan or programme
I am applying for the vendor registration advertised on your website on 3 March 2025.
Introduce your business to a new organisation
I would like to introduce Grace Prints, a printing business in Enugu serving schools and churches.
Report a problem and request a remedy
I am writing about a faulty generator, receipt number 0458, bought on 2 March 2025.
I am writing to confirm the terms we agreed at our meeting on 10 March 2025.

blocks.text: Notice that every first sentence states the purpose directly, the same rule you learned for emails and WhatsApp messages.

takeaways: Full block format puts every part at the left margin.
Write the date in full to avoid day-month confusion.
Dear Mr or Mrs Name pairs with Yours sincerely; Dear Sir or Madam pairs with Yours faithfully.
A good complaint letter gives facts, evidence, a fair request and a deadline.
Ask reviewers specific questions, and learn from the follow-up questions readers send you.

steps: Choose a real need for a formal letter: enquiry, application, complaint or introduction.
Type it in full block format, with the date written in full and a subject line.
Check that your salutation and complimentary close match.
Give it to one trusted reader with the five review questions.
Revise it based on their answers.

quiz.q: Which subject line is most effective for an email requesting a quote?
options: Quotation request: 200 branded mugs, needed by 30 April
quiz.explain: It tells the reader exactly what the email is about and the deadline before they open it.

quiz.q: Tola emails 40 customers about new stock. Most do not know each other. Where should their addresses go?
quiz.explain: BCC hides recipients' addresses from each other, protecting customer privacy.

quiz.q: A customer asks "How much is the red bag?" on WhatsApp. Which reply is best?
options: Available, ₦5,000, delivery in Lagos about ₦1,500 in 1 to 2 days, pay by transfer. Would you like to order?
quiz.explain: A complete reply covers availability, price, delivery and payment and ends with a clear question.

quiz.q: A customer sends a screenshot of a transfer for ₦20,000 and asks you to dispatch now. What should you do first?
options: Dispatch immediately, the screenshot is proof
Check your own banking app or bank SMS to confirm the money arrived
Ask them to send the screenshot again
Ask for a voice note confirming payment
quiz.explain: Screenshots can be faked. Only your own bank record confirms payment.

quiz.q: A letter begins "Dear Sir or Madam". Which close is correct in British-style business English?
quiz.explain: When you do not name the reader, the matching close is Yours faithfully.

quiz.q: Why write "14 March 2025" instead of "03/14/25" or "14/03/25" in a business letter?
options: It looks longer and more formal
Some readers put the month first and others the day, so numbers alone can be misread
quiz.explain: Writing the month as a word removes any day-month confusion between readers.

modules.title: Quality and Evidence: Money Documents, Meetings and Trust
modules.overview: Some business communication creates records that others rely on: invoices, receipts, meeting minutes and written promises. This module teaches you to word these documents precisely, run and record meetings so decisions actually happen, and communicate honestly and safely when things go wrong.

lessons.title: Wording quotations, invoices, receipts and payment reminders
objectives: Explain the difference between a quotation, an invoice and a receipt
List the details every invoice and receipt should contain
Write clear payment terms and polite, firm payment reminders
Protect your business from common payment scams

blocks.text: Money documents are communication too. A vague invoice leads to late payment, arguments about what was agreed, and lost money. A clear one gets paid faster because the customer, or their accounts department, has everything needed to pay without asking questions. These documents are also your business records, which you will need for tax, loans and grant applications.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.caption: Clear money documents get you paid faster and protect you in disputes.

blocks.text: Three documents, three jobs

blocks.title: From enquiry to payment
items: Quotation: the offer
Customer accepts
Invoice: request to pay
Payment received
Receipt: proof of payment
blocks.caption: Each document has its own moment and its own job in the sale.

head: Document
When you send it
What it says
rows: "This is what we will supply and what it will cost, valid until a date"
Before payment, when a customer needs a formal document to approve or release funds
A preliminary invoice showing the expected charges
After the order is agreed or delivered
"Please pay this amount, by this date, to this account"
"We have received this amount, on this date, for these goods or services"

blocks.text: What every invoice should include

items: The word INVOICE and a unique invoice number (for example INV-2025-014), so payments can be matched
Invoice date and payment due date
Your business name, address, phone, email and, if registered, your CAC registration number
The customer's name or company and address
A line for each item: description, quantity, unit price and line total
Subtotal, any delivery charge or discount, any tax that applies to you, and the total amount due in figures
Payment terms and your bank account name, bank and account number
A short thank-you line

blocks.text: **Payment terms** tell the customer exactly when to pay. Use clear phrases such as "Due on receipt", "Payment due within 7 days of invoice date" or "50% deposit to confirm, balance on delivery". Avoid "pay as soon as possible", which means something different to every reader. If tax applies to your business, show it on its own line, and check current rules with a qualified accountant or the tax authority rather than guessing.

blocks.title: Worked example: an invoice line, before and after
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma runs a tailoring business in Port Harcourt and has sewn uniforms for a small private school.
steps: Before: "Uniforms. ₦480,000. Pay soon." The school bursar cannot tell how many uniforms, what sizes, or when payment is due, and puts it aside.
After, invoice number and dates: "INVOICE INV-2025-009. Date: 3 March 2025. Due: 10 March 2025."
After, item lines: "Girls' pinafore, sizes 6 to 12: 40 at ₦6,500 = ₦260,000. Boys' shirt and shorts set, sizes 6 to 12: 40 at ₦5,500 = ₦220,000."
After, totals and terms: "Total due: ₦480,000. Deposit paid 10 February: ₦240,000. Balance due: ₦240,000 within 7 days. Pay to: Ifeoma Stitches, [bank name], [account number]."
blocks.result: The bursar can approve the balance of ₦240,000 immediately because every number is shown and adds up.

blocks.text: Receipts

A receipt should say RECEIPT, have its own number, the date, who paid, the amount in figures and in words ("Two hundred and forty thousand naira only"), what it was for, the payment method, and your name or signature. Writing the amount in words makes it harder for anyone to alter the figure.
Polite, firm payment reminders

items: Day before due date (friendly): "Good morning Mrs Ade, a quick reminder that invoice INV-2025-009 for ₦240,000 is due tomorrow, 10 March. Thank you."
A few days late (clear): "Invoice INV-2025-009 for ₦240,000 was due on 10 March. Please let me know when payment will be made. I have attached it again."
Two weeks late (firm): "Invoice INV-2025-009 for ₦240,000 is now 14 days overdue. Please pay by Friday 28 March, or call me today so we can agree a payment plan."

blocks.title: Payment scams to watch for
blocks.text: Fraudsters send fake transfer alerts by SMS and fake screenshots. Confirm every payment in your own banking app before releasing goods. If a supplier suddenly sends "new bank details", call them on a number you already have to check before paying. Never share your OTP, PIN or BVN with anyone who contacts you.
Sending and keeping invoices

items: Send invoices as PDF files so the figures cannot be changed easily, and name them clearly, for example INV-2025-009_Ifeoma_Stitches.pdf.
In the message, state the total and the due date in the text, not only inside the attachment.
Keep a copy of every invoice and receipt, in a folder on your phone, in cloud storage or in a printed file, in number order.
Record each invoice in a simple sales book or spreadsheet with its number, customer, amount, due date and the date it was paid.

takeaways: A quote is the offer, an invoice requests payment, a receipt proves payment.
Number every invoice and receipt and show each item, quantity and price.
Use exact payment terms such as "due within 7 days".
Write receipt amounts in figures and words.
Confirm payments in your own banking app before releasing goods.

activity.title: Create your invoice and receipt templates
steps: Using a free app such as Google Docs, Google Sheets or an invoicing app, create an invoice template with every item from the checklist.
Create a matching receipt template with amount in figures and words.
Fill in both for a real or realistic recent sale and check all the arithmetic.
Write your three payment reminder messages and save them as WhatsApp quick replies.
activity.evidence: A completed sample invoice, a matching receipt, and your three saved reminder messages

lessons.title: Running meetings and writing minutes that lead to action
objectives: Prepare and share a simple agenda before a meeting
Keep a meeting focused and on time as chair
Write action-focused minutes with decisions, owners and deadlines
Send minutes promptly and follow up on action items

blocks.text: Cooperative meetings, women's association meetings, partner meetings and team meetings can either move a business forward or waste an afternoon. The difference is usually preparation and follow-up. A good meeting has a clear purpose before it starts, and clear decisions and actions in writing after it ends.

blocks.name: meeting
blocks.alt: People seated around a table in a meeting
blocks.caption: A clear agenda before and clear minutes after turn talk into action.

blocks.text: Before: the agenda

An **agenda** is a short list of what the meeting will cover, shared in advance. Send it at least a day before, even if only on WhatsApp. Include the date, time, place or video link, the purpose, and a list of items, each with the person leading it and a rough time. Putting a time on each item stops one topic from eating the whole meeting.

head: Agenda item
Lead
Time
rows: 3. Decide: join the trade fair in April?

blocks.text: During: chairing well

items: Start on time, even if a few people are late; this teaches everyone that time matters.
State the purpose in one sentence at the start.
Keep to the agenda; when a new topic comes up, note it for "any other business" or a future meeting.
Give quieter members a chance: "Mama Chidi, what do you think?"
At the end of each item, say the decision out loud so the secretary records it correctly.
Before closing, read out every action item with its owner and deadline.

blocks.text: After: minutes that lead to action

**Minutes** are the official written record of a meeting. Small businesses and groups rarely need word-for-word notes. **Action minutes** are better: they record who attended, the main points briefly, what was decided, and who will do what by when. An action without an owner and a deadline usually does not happen.

blocks.title: What good minutes record
items: Date, time, place
Present and apologies
Decisions made
Actions: owner and deadline
Next meeting date
blocks.caption: If your minutes contain these five things, anyone who missed the meeting knows exactly what happens next.

blocks.title: Worked example: minutes, before and after
blocks.context: For example, a women's farming cooperative in Benue meets to decide whether to rent a stand at a trade fair. Their secretary, Doose, takes notes.
steps: Before: "We talked about the trade fair. Everybody liked the idea. Money was discussed. We will see." No decision, no owner, no deadline.
After, heading: "Minutes of the monthly meeting, Iyange Women Farmers Cooperative, Saturday 8 February 2025, 4pm, community hall. Present: 14 members. Apologies: 2."

After, item 3: "Trade fair, April. Stand rental is about ₦60,000 (approximate, to be confirmed). Decision: the cooperative will take a stand if the fee is confirmed at ₦60,000 or less. Agreed by 12 of 14 members present."

After, actions: "Doose to confirm the stand fee with the organisers by 15 February. Treasurer to report the available balance in the WhatsApp group by 15 February. Mercy to list products and quantities for the stand by 22 February."
After, close: "Next meeting: Saturday 8 March, 4pm, same venue."
blocks.result: Everyone knows what was decided, who is responsible and by when, and at the next meeting the chair can simply check each action.

items: Write up the minutes within 24 to 48 hours, while memory is fresh.
Share them with all members, including those who were absent.
Start the next meeting by checking each action from the last minutes.
Keep all minutes together in one folder or notebook as the group's record.

blocks.title: Online meetings
blocks.text: For meetings on Zoom, Google Meet or WhatsApp video, send the link with the agenda, ask people to mute when not speaking, and use the chat to collect decisions and actions as you go. Ask permission before recording, and say clearly how the recording will be stored and used.
Taking notes during the meeting

The secretary does not need to write every sentence. Prepare a page in advance with the agenda items as headings, and under each one leave space for three things: key points, decision, and actions. Write names and figures exactly. If a decision is unclear, it is the secretary's job to ask: "So what have we decided, and who will do it?" That one question saves many arguments later.

head: Under each agenda item
What to write
rows: Two or three short lines, not a full conversation
Exactly what was agreed, and the vote if one was taken

blocks.text: When the minutes are ready, the chair should read them before they are shared, to check that every decision is recorded as agreed. At the next meeting, members confirm the minutes as a true record, and any corrections are noted. This simple habit makes the minutes trusted, so they can settle later disagreements about what was decided.

takeaways: Send a short agenda with times at least a day before.
The chair keeps time, keeps focus and says each decision out loud.
Action minutes record decisions, owners and deadlines, not every word.
Share minutes within 48 hours and check actions at the next meeting.

activity.title: Agenda and minutes for a real meeting
steps: Choose a real upcoming meeting: team, cooperative, association or family business.
Write and share an agenda with items, leads and times.
Take notes during the meeting focused on decisions and actions.
Write action minutes using the five-part checklist and share them within 48 hours.
activity.evidence: The shared agenda and the final minutes with at least two actions, each with an owner and deadline

lessons.title: Honest promises, confidentiality and handling complaints
objectives: Make written commitments you can actually keep
Protect customer and partner information in line with data protection principles
Respond to a complaint using a calm, structured method
Deliver bad news early and clearly

blocks.text: Trust is built slowly and lost quickly. In business communication, three things damage trust more than anything else: promising what you cannot deliver, being careless with other people's information, and responding badly when something goes wrong. This lesson gives you practical habits for all three.

blocks.name: handshake
blocks.caption: Honest promises and careful handling of information keep the trust behind every deal.

blocks.text: Promise only what you can deliver

It is tempting to say yes to a big order or a fast deadline to win the job. But a written promise, whether a price, a quantity or a delivery date, is something the customer will plan around and may hold you to. Before you commit in writing, check your stock, your suppliers, your time and your cash. If you are not sure, say what you **can** commit to and when you will confirm the rest.

head: Over-promise
Honest commitment
rows: "We can deliver 300 packs by Friday and the remaining 200 by Tuesday. Does that work?"
"We have supplied 12 schools in Enugu over the last two years." (only if true)

blocks.text: Confidentiality and personal data

Customers trust you with their names, phone numbers, addresses and sometimes payment details. Nigeria's **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, sets rules for how organisations collect and use personal data. Even as a small business, the safe habits are simple: collect only what you need, use it only for the reason you collected it, keep it secure, and do not share it without permission.

items: Do not forward a customer's phone number or address to anyone who does not need it to deliver their order.
Do not post screenshots of customer chats or receipts showing names, numbers or account details.
Do not tell one client about another client's prices, orders or problems.
Lock your phone and laptop with a PIN or password, and turn on two-step verification for WhatsApp and email.

blocks.text: Handling a complaint: the LAST method

Complaints are a chance to keep a customer for life, or to lose them and everyone they talk to. A widely taught customer-service approach is often summarised as **LAST**: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank. Apologising for the customer's experience is not the same as admitting legal fault; it shows you take them seriously.

blocks.title: The LAST complaint method
items: Listen fully
Apologise sincerely
Solve with a clear offer
Thank and follow up
blocks.caption: Work through each step in order, and the follow-up brings the customer back to trusting you.

blocks.title: Worked example: replying to an angry customer
blocks.context: For example, Blessing sells baked goods in Warri. A customer sends: "The cake you delivered for my daughter's birthday was squashed and the writing was spoilt. I am very disappointed."
steps: Listen: Blessing reads the whole message, asks for a photo, and does not argue about the delivery rider.
Apologise: "I am truly sorry, Mrs Efe. Your daughter's birthday cake should have arrived perfect, and I understand how disappointing this was."
Solve: "I would like to make it right. I can refund 50% (₦12,500 of the ₦25,000) today, or bake a fresh cake of the same size free of charge for any date you choose. Which would you prefer?"
Thank: "Thank you for telling me directly. It helps me fix our packaging." She later changes to a sturdier box and checks every cake before it leaves.
Follow up: a week later she messages: "I hope the replacement cake was enjoyed. Thank you again for giving us another chance."
blocks.result: The customer chooses the replacement cake, stays loyal, and Blessing fixes the real cause of the problem.

blocks.text: Delivering bad news

If a delivery will be late or a price must rise, tell the customer **as early as possible**, with the reason in one sentence, the new plan and what you are doing to help. "Your order will arrive Thursday instead of Tuesday because our supplier's truck broke down. I have arranged express delivery at no extra cost." Silence, followed by excuses after the deadline, does far more damage.

blocks.title: Stay professional when others are not
blocks.text: If someone insults you in a message, do not reply in anger. Wait, then reply calmly with facts and a next step. Your written replies can be screenshotted and shared, so write every message as if others may one day read it.
Phrases for difficult messages

items: Acknowledging: "Thank you for letting me know. I understand why this is frustrating."
Taking responsibility: "This was our mistake, and I am sorry."
Giving time to check: "Let me look into this and reply by 4pm today."
Offering choice: "Would you prefer a refund or a replacement?"
Closing warmly: "Thank you for your patience. We value your business."

takeaways: Check stock, time and cash before you commit in writing.
Collect, use and share customer data only for the reason it was given.
Handle complaints with Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank.
Give bad news early, with a reason and a new plan.
Write every message as if it could be shared publicly.

activity.title: Prepare your trust toolkit
steps: Write a short data rule for your business: what customer details you collect, why, and who can see them.
Draft a LAST reply to a realistic complaint in your type of business.
Draft a bad-news message for a late delivery, with reason, new plan and goodwill gesture.
Review one recent promise you made in writing and check you can keep it.

quiz.q: A school asks for a document showing expected charges so the bursar can approve funds before ordering. What should you send?
quiz.explain: A proforma invoice shows the expected charges before payment so the customer can approve the spending.

quiz.q: An invoice shows 30 items at ₦4,500 and a deposit of ₦50,000 already paid. What balance is due?
Which payment term is clearest?
options: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date
quiz.explain: It gives an exact period, so the due date cannot be misunderstood.

quiz.q: Which line from meeting minutes is written best?
options: Ada to confirm the stand fee with organisers by 15 February
quiz.explain: A good action item has an owner, a specific task and a deadline.

quiz.q: A customer complains that an order arrived damaged. Using LAST, what comes right after listening?
options: Explain that the rider was at fault
Offer a discount on the next order only

quiz.q: A supplier messages: "Our bank has changed, please pay the ₦300,000 to this new account." What should you do?

Call the supplier on a number you already have to confirm before paying
