modules.title: Portfolio and Impact: Negotiation, Cultures and Your Capstone
modules.overview: In the final module you take your skills into two higher-stakes areas, negotiating with suppliers and customers and communicating across cultures, and then bring everything together in a capstone project with measurable results and a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Negotiation basics: prepare, listen and agree in writing
objectives: Prepare for a negotiation by setting your target, walk-away point and alternative
Tell the difference between a position and an interest
Use the four principles of principled negotiation in a real conversation
Close a negotiation with a clear written summary

blocks.text: Every business negotiates all the time: with suppliers on price, with landlords on rent, with customers on discounts, with partners on who does what. Negotiation is not about shouting or tricks. Good negotiation is mostly **preparation, listening and clear communication**, so both sides leave with an agreement they will keep.

blocks.name: business-deal
blocks.alt: Two business people agreeing a deal
blocks.caption: Good negotiation ends with an agreement both sides are willing to keep.

blocks.text: The principled negotiation method

One of the best-known approaches comes from Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project, in their book **Getting to Yes**. They describe four principles. First, **separate the people from the problem**: be respectful to the person while being firm on the issue. Second, **focus on interests, not positions**. Third, **invent options for mutual gain** before deciding. Fourth, **insist on objective criteria**, such as market prices or published rates, rather than pressure.
Positions and interests

A **position** is what someone says they want: "I want ₦50,000 off." An **interest** is why they want it: "My cash is tight this month" or "I need to stay within my client's budget." When you find the interest, you can often find a solution that the position hides, such as splitting payment, changing the quantity or adjusting delivery.
Prepare three numbers and one alternative

head: Term
Meaning
Example for a buyer
rows: The realistic result you are aiming for
Buy 100 bags of rice at about ₦68,000 each
The worst deal you will accept; beyond this you say no
Where you start, close enough to be taken seriously
Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will do if there is no deal

blocks.text: The term **BATNA** comes from Getting to Yes. The stronger your alternative, the more confidently you can negotiate, because you do not need this particular deal. Always find at least one real alternative before an important negotiation. (All prices here are illustrative only.)

blocks.title: Five steps of a negotiation
items: Prepare numbers and BATNA
Ask and listen
Find the interests
Offer options
Confirm in writing
blocks.caption: Most of the work happens before and after the conversation, not during it.

blocks.title: Worked example: negotiating a bulk fabric price
blocks.context: For example, Zainab makes ready-to-wear dresses in Kaduna and buys Ankara fabric from one wholesaler. She wants a better price for a larger, regular order. All figures are illustrative.
steps: Preparation: current price about ₦9,000 per 6-yard piece. Target ₦8,200. Walk-away ₦8,600. BATNA: another wholesaler in the same market quoted ₦8,500, but with slower delivery.
Opening: "I have bought from you for a year and I am planning to order 50 pieces every month instead of 20. Could you give me a price of ₦8,000 per piece for that volume?"
Listening: the wholesaler says ₦8,000 is too low because he must pay for transport from Lagos. Zainab asks: "What would help you most?" He says: payment on time and fewer small orders.
Options: Zainab offers to pay the full amount on collection and order once a month. He offers ₦8,300.
Agreement: they settle at ₦8,300 for orders of 50 pieces or more, paid on collection. Saving: (₦9,000 − ₦8,300) × 50 = ₦35,000 per month.
Written summary on WhatsApp: "Thank you. Confirming: 50 pieces or more per month at ₦8,300 per piece, full payment on collection, starting April."
blocks.result: By understanding the wholesaler's interest in reliable payment and fewer small orders, Zainab reached a price inside her target range and a written agreement both can rely on.

blocks.text: Useful phrases

items: To open: "Based on the volume I am offering, I would like to discuss the price."
To understand interests: "What matters most to you in this order?"
To use objective criteria: "Other suppliers in the market are quoting around ₦8,500. How can we get closer?"
To trade, not give away: "If I pay in full on collection, can you do ₦8,300?"
To pause: "Let me think about this and reply by tomorrow at noon."

blocks.title: Silence and time are allowed
blocks.text: You do not have to answer an offer immediately. Saying "Let me check my numbers and get back to you by tomorrow" is professional and protects you from agreeing to something below your walk-away point.
Common mistakes to avoid

items: Negotiating without knowing your walk-away point, then agreeing to a price that loses money.
Revealing your deadline pressure too early: "I need it today at any price."
Giving a discount without asking for anything in return, such as faster payment or a bigger order.
Making personal attacks or showing anger, which turns a problem into a quarrel.
Leaving the agreement only verbal, so each side remembers it differently a month later.

takeaways: Prepare a target, a walk-away point, an opening offer and your BATNA.
Look for the interest behind every position.
Separate the person from the problem and use objective criteria.
Trade concessions instead of giving them away.
End every negotiation with a written summary.

activity.title: Plan and hold one real negotiation
steps: Choose a real negotiation: a supplier price, rent, a client fee or delivery terms.
Write your target, walk-away point, opening offer and BATNA.
List two interests you think the other side has.
Hold the conversation using at least two of the useful phrases.
Send a written summary of whatever was agreed.
activity.evidence: Your preparation sheet and a screenshot of the written summary

lessons.title: Communicating across cultures, languages and time zones
objectives: Explain the difference between high-context and low-context communication
Adapt greetings, directness and timing for different cultural expectations
Write simple, clear English for readers who use it as a second language
Schedule calls and set deadlines correctly across time zones

blocks.text: Nigeria alone has hundreds of languages and many cultural traditions, and African businesses increasingly trade across borders and online with buyers in Europe, America and Asia. The same words can be heard as polite in one setting and rude in another. Cross-cultural communication means noticing these differences and adjusting, without stereotyping anyone.

blocks.name: around-the-world
blocks.caption: Clear communication travels across cultures when you adjust to your reader.

blocks.text: High-context and low-context communication

The anthropologist Edward T. Hall described cultures as tending towards **high-context** or **low-context** communication. In high-context settings, much of the meaning is in the relationship, the setting and what is not said directly. In low-context settings, people expect meaning to be stated plainly in the words themselves. Many West African business settings lean towards high context; many Northern European and American business settings lean towards low context. These are tendencies, not rules about every person.

blocks.title: Two communication styles
items: High-context
Low-context
blocks.caption: Neither style is better; misunderstandings happen when each side expects its own style.

head: Situation
What can go wrong
How to adjust
rows: A Nigerian supplier emails a German buyer with long greetings and family wishes
The buyer may see it as slow to get to the point
Keep a warm opening line, then state the business clearly
A buyer abroad writes "Send the samples by Friday." with no greeting
It can feel rude or cold to a Nigerian reader
Read it as normal directness in their style, not disrespect
A partner says "We will try our best" instead of no
A low-context reader may think it means yes
Ask a gentle, specific question: "Should I plan for Friday or the following week?"
Meeting an older community leader for the first time
Rushing into business can seem disrespectful
Take time for greetings and respect titles before the request

blocks.text: Writing for second-language readers

items: Use short sentences and common words.
Avoid idioms and slang such as "ball is in your court", "no wahala" or "I am on seat".
Write dates with the month as a word (15 April 2025) and always show the currency with amounts (₦50,000, or the currency you have agreed with the buyer).
Spell out abbreviations the first time: "Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)".
Use lists for steps or several items.
Check the reply: if they answer a different question, your message may have been unclear.

blocks.text: Time zones and timing

Nigeria uses **West Africa Time (WAT)**, which is one hour ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC+1), with no daylight saving changes. The United Kingdom is one hour behind Nigeria in winter and the same time as Nigeria in summer, because the UK changes its clocks. The east coast of the United States is five or six hours behind Nigeria, depending on the season. When you propose a call abroad, **state both times**.

blocks.title: Worked example: scheduling a call with a buyer abroad
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka exports shea butter from Abuja and needs a video call with a buyer in New York in winter, when New York is six hours behind Nigeria.
steps: Her working hours: 9am to 6pm WAT. Converted to New York in winter: 3am to 12 noon.
A good overlap: 3pm WAT is 9am in New York, early in the buyer's day.
Her message: "Dear Ms Carter, could we have a 30-minute video call on Tuesday 14 January at 9am New York time (3pm in Nigeria, WAT)? I will send a Google Meet link."
She checks the time in a world clock app before sending, and adds the call to her calendar with both times.
Deadline wording: "Please send the signed order by Friday 17 January, 5pm New York time."
blocks.result: Because both times are stated, neither side misses the call or a deadline because of a time difference.

blocks.title: Respect is universal, style is local
blocks.text: When unsure, be polite, clear and patient, ask questions rather than assume, and follow the other person's lead on formality, greetings and directness. Most people welcome a sincere effort to understand their style.
Names, greetings and video calls

Learn how people want to be addressed and how to pronounce their names; asking politely is a sign of respect, not ignorance. Greetings matter greatly in many Nigerian communities, and taking a moment to greet properly before business is often expected. With international contacts, a short, friendly greeting is usually enough before moving to the agenda.

items: On video calls with people abroad, join a few minutes early and test your internet and microphone.
Speak a little more slowly than usual and pause for questions.
Send a short written summary after the call, because spoken accents can make details easy to mishear.
Check public holidays in the other country before setting dates.

takeaways: High-context communication relies on relationship and setting; low-context relies on explicit words.
Adjust greetings and directness to your reader, without stereotyping.
Use simple English and avoid idioms with second-language readers.
Nigeria is on WAT (UTC+1); always state both times for calls abroad.
Ask clarifying questions instead of assuming meaning.

activity.title: Adapt one message for a different culture
steps: Choose a message you might send to a business contact from a different culture or country.
Write it first in your natural style.
Rewrite it in simple English, removing idioms and adjusting the greeting and directness.
If the contact is abroad, add a proposed time in both time zones, checked with a world clock app.
activity.evidence: Both versions of the message, with notes on what you changed and why

lessons.title: Your capstone: real messages, measured results and a 90-day plan
objectives: Produce a complete, professional business message for a real purpose
Keep a simple communication log that measures response rate and follow-up questions
Explain your communication choices using the principles from this course
Write a specific 90-day practice plan

blocks.text: This final lesson brings the course together. You will produce one real piece of business communication, measure how your messages perform, and plan how you will keep improving. Your evidence is what makes your certificate meaningful: it shows you can apply these skills, not only describe them.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a portfolio of work
blocks.caption: Your capstone portfolio shows real, applied communication skill.

blocks.text: Step 1: choose a real purpose

Pick a message that matters to your business right now: a first email to a potential client, a quotation, a letter to a programme or office, a negotiation summary with a supplier, or a payment reminder. Real purposes give you real feedback, which is far more valuable than a practice exercise.
Step 2: build it with the course checklist

blocks.title: Capstone quality checklist
items: Purpose in first lines
Right tone and format
Every detail named
One clear request
Proofread and checked
blocks.caption: Check your capstone against each point before you send it.

blocks.text: Step 3: keep a communication log

A **communication log** is a simple table, in a notebook or a spreadsheet, where you record important messages and what happened. Over a few weeks it shows you real patterns: which messages get replies, which ones cause confusion, and how long people take to respond.

Two simple measures help most. **Response rate**: how many important messages got a reply, divided by how many you sent. **Clarification rate**: how many replies asked a question your message should have answered. As your writing improves, the first should rise and the second should fall.

blocks.title: Worked example: measuring improvement
blocks.context: For example, Ruth runs a cleaning service in Lagos and logs her client messages for four weeks before and four weeks after this course.
steps: Before: 20 important messages sent, 11 replies. Response rate: 11 ÷ 20 = 55%. Of the 11 replies, 6 asked for missing details (price, date or address). Clarification rate: 6 ÷ 11, about 55%.
Changes she made: purpose-first openings, complete WhatsApp replies with price and availability, specific subject lines, and payment terms on every invoice.
After: 20 important messages sent, 16 replies. Response rate: 16 ÷ 20 = 80%. Of the 16 replies, 3 asked for missing details. Clarification rate: 3 ÷ 16, about 19%.
She writes this in her capstone reflection with copies of two before-and-after messages.
blocks.result: Ruth has clear, honest evidence of improvement that she can show a mentor, a client or a programme officer.

blocks.text: Step 4: explain your choices

In a short reflection of about 150 to 300 words, explain why you made your choices: why this channel, this level of formality, this subject line and this request. If you sent the message, record the response. If you did not, explain what response you expect and why. Be honest about what you would still improve.
Step 5: your 90-day plan

items: Name one type of communication to practise, such as client emails, invoices, negotiation or meetings.
Set a measurable goal, such as raising your response rate or sending minutes within 48 hours every time.
Choose how often you will practise, such as two important messages a week reviewed against the checklist.
Name one person who will give you feedback, and when.
Set review dates at 30, 60 and 90 days to check your log.

blocks.title: Showing your skill to others
blocks.text: When applying for a role, grant or contract, a short example is stronger than a claim. Instead of "I am a good communicator", say "After restructuring my client emails, my response rate rose from about half to about four in five over eight weeks", and be ready to show a sample message.
A sample 90-day plan

head: Period
Focus
Measure
rows: Purpose-first client emails and complete WhatsApp replies
Log every important message; note response rate
Numbered invoices with clear payment terms and reminders
One planned negotiation with a supplier, confirmed in writing
Record the saving or improved terms

blocks.text: Presenting your portfolio

Arrange your capstone folder in a clear order: the final message first, then the before version, the response or your reasoning, the log, the reflection and the plan. Give each item a short label. If you share it digitally, combine the items into one PDF with a clear file name, for example Ruth_Capstone_BusinessCommunication.pdf, so a reviewer on a phone can open it in one tap.
Keep the plan where you will see it, such as pinned in your notebook or saved as a phone note, and ask your feedback partner to check in at each review date.

takeaways: Use a real business purpose for your capstone.
Check every message against the five-point quality checklist.
Track response rate and clarification rate in a simple log.
Explain your choices honestly in a short reflection.
Turn your learning into a specific, measurable 90-day plan.

activity.title: Assemble your capstone portfolio
steps: Write and, if possible, send your capstone message.
Start your communication log and record at least five important messages.
Write your 150 to 300 word reflection explaining your choices.
Write your 90-day plan with a measurable goal and review dates.
Put all items in one folder (paper or digital).
activity.evidence: Your capstone message, log, reflection and 90-day plan in one folder

quiz.q: A landlord says "I want ₦100,000 more rent this year." Which is his interest rather than his position?
quiz.explain: The position is the demand; the interest is the reason behind it, which opens room for other solutions.

quiz.q: Zainab's walk-away price is ₦8,600 per piece. The supplier's final offer is ₦8,900 and another supplier offers ₦8,500. What should she do?
options: Decline and use her alternative at ₦8,500
quiz.explain: The offer is above her walk-away point, and her BATNA of ₦8,500 is better, so she should use it.

quiz.q: What does BATNA stand for?
options: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement
quiz.explain: BATNA is the Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement, the term introduced in Getting to Yes.

quiz.q: A partner from a high-context culture replies "We will try our best" to your Friday deadline. What is the best next step?
options: Assume it means no and cancel
Ask a gentle, specific question about which date to plan for
Send the deadline again in capital letters
quiz.explain: Indirect answers can hide a no. A polite, specific question clarifies without causing loss of face.

quiz.q: It is winter and New York is six hours behind Nigeria. You want a call at 10am New York time. What time is that in Nigeria (WAT)?
quiz.explain: 10am plus six hours is 4pm WAT.

quiz.q: Ruth sent 25 important messages and got 15 replies. What is her response rate?

finalQuiz.q: Which opening best follows the purpose-first rule?
options: I hope this finds you well. As you may recall, some time ago we spoke about many things
Please send the invoice for the Main Hall for Saturday 29 March
Greetings to you and your family, I trust all is well
It has come to my attention that
finalQuiz.explain: It states the request immediately, with the exact hall and date.

finalQuiz.q: You are emailing a government office for the first time and do not know the officer's name. Which pair is correct?
options: Dear Sir or Madam ... Yours sincerely
Dear Sir or Madam ... Yours faithfully
finalQuiz.explain: An unnamed formal reader takes Dear Sir or Madam with Yours faithfully.

finalQuiz.q: A customer calls to order cupcakes. What should you do before ending the call?
options: Hang up quickly to save airtime
Repeat back the quantity, date and time, then agree the next step
Ask them to call back tomorrow
Send a voice note of three minutes
finalQuiz.explain: Repeating key details catches misunderstandings, and agreeing the next step moves the order forward.

finalQuiz.q: Who belongs in the CC line of an email?
options: The person who must take action
People who only need to be informed
Customers who do not know each other
finalQuiz.explain: To is for action, CC is for information, BCC protects private addresses.

finalQuiz.q: Which WhatsApp Business tool lets you send a saved price list by typing a short shortcut?
finalQuiz.explain: Quick replies are saved answers you insert by typing / and the shortcut.

finalQuiz.q: An invoice lists 25 items at ₦3,200 and delivery of ₦5,000. What is the total due?
Why should a receipt show the amount in words as well as figures?
options: It makes the amount harder to alter
Banks require it for every transfer
It replaces the need for a receipt number
finalQuiz.explain: Writing the amount in words makes it much harder for anyone to change the figure.

finalQuiz.q: Which minutes entry will most likely lead to action?
options: The fair was discussed at length
Treasurer to share the bank balance in the group by 15 February
finalQuiz.explain: It names the person, the task and the deadline.

finalQuiz.q: A buyer from a low-context culture writes: "Send the samples by Friday." with no greeting. What is the best interpretation?
options: The buyer is being rude on purpose
This is a normal direct style; reply clearly and confirm the date
Ignore the message until they greet you
finalQuiz.explain: Low-context communicators often state requests plainly. It is a style difference, not disrespect.

finalQuiz.q: Before a rent negotiation, Hauwa finds another shop at ₦600,000 a year. In negotiation terms, this shop is her:
finalQuiz.explain: Her best alternative if no agreement is reached is her BATNA.

finalQuiz.q: A large order will be three days late because of a supplier problem. When should you tell the customer?
options: As soon as you know, with the reason and a new plan
Never; deliver late and apologise then
finalQuiz.explain: Bad news delivered early, with a reason and a plan, protects trust far better than silence.

finalQuiz.q: Over four weeks you sent 30 important messages and 9 replies asked for details you had left out. What should you change first?
options: Add the missing details, such as prices, dates and totals, to your first messages
finalQuiz.explain: Frequent clarification questions show your first messages are incomplete. Adding the details reduces back and forth.

capstone.title: Professional Business Communication Project
capstone.brief: Produce one complete, professional business message for a real purpose (an email, letter, quotation, invoice with reminder, or negotiation summary), document the response or explain your choices in a short reflection, show a four-week communication log, and write a 90-day practice plan.
steps: Choose a real business purpose that matters to you now.
Draft the message using the right channel, format and level of formality.
Check it against the five-point quality checklist and ask one person for feedback using specific questions.
Send it if possible and record the response in your communication log.
Write a 150 to 300 word reflection explaining your choices and what you would improve.
Write a 90-day plan with one focus, a measurable goal, a feedback partner and review dates.
evidence: The final message, with a before version if you rewrote an earlier one
Screenshot or note of the response received, or your reasoning if not sent
A communication log of at least five important messages with response and clarification notes
